This week, Substack gave readers a new button.

Posts, Notes, comments, and replies can now be scanned for AI-assisted text, with a percentage estimating how much appears human-written and how much appears machine-assisted. Writers can also add a public statement explaining how they make their work.

The feature arrives for an obvious reason. Readers know the internet is filling with polished work that may contain very little human thought behind it.

But a detector can only examine the text in front of it. It cannot tell you whether the writer understood the subject, verified the sources, noticed the larger pattern, resisted a convenient lie, or would still stand behind the conclusion once someone acted on it.

That is the actual problem.

“Does not the ear test words, as the palate tastes food?” - Job 12:11 (BLB)

Every technological revolution makes some skills cheaper and makes others more valuable. The printing press made memorization cheap and made literacy valuable. The internet made information abundant and made attention scarce. Artificial intelligence is making a wide layer of cognitive output cheap: first drafts, first-pass analysis, competent prose on any subject, produced at the price of electricity.

So what becomes scarce now?

Not information. Not a fluent draft. Not the basic analysis a machine can already do as well as most people, and faster. What stays scarce is the analysis someone is willing to put their name on, and everything that has to stand behind it once it’s used: the judgment to test it, the sense to know what it means across more than one field, the fluency to use the tool itself without handing it your judgment along with your labor, the trust that makes a sentence worth acting on, and the character to own what gets built with all of it. Five things. Only one of them didn’t exist as a named skill a generation ago.

1. Judgment and Verification

A claim can now be generated faster than it can be tested. Twenty arguments in ten seconds, each one grammatically clean, each one sourced enough to sound sourced. The old defense against a bad argument was time. You had to sit with it, turn it over, find the seam. That defense is gone. The seam gets stitched shut before you finish reading.

Judgment is what’s left, and it’s bigger than it used to be. It isn’t only weighing a claim once. It’s testing the claim, testing the source behind it, and testing what the source cites in its own defense, before any of it gets repeated. Paul told the church in Thessalonica to test all things and hold fast to what is good. That’s not a librarian’s instruction. It’s the discipline of rejecting most of what passes in front of you instead of accepting it because it arrived polished.

Paul told Timothy something related. God did not give him a spirit of timidity, but of power and love and soundness of mind. Timidity and haste do the same work. They let a claim land before the testing judgment requires has a seat at the table. Soundness of mind isn’t a mood. It’s a discipline exercised before the pressure arrives, because it can’t be improvised once the pressure is already in the room.

A machine can generate the case. It can even generate a citation for the case. It was never going to be asked to carry the verdict.

2. AI Literacy and Tool Stewardship

The tool wasn’t built neutral, and pretending it was is its own kind of carelessness. It came out of a system with its own incentives, trained on a world with its own distortions, and it will reflect both unless someone who understands that stands between it and the output. The real question was never whether to touch it. Scripture already answered a harder version of that question.

On the way out of Egypt, the people of Israel asked their former captors for silver, gold, and clothing, and the Egyptians, undone by the plagues, handed it over. Scripture doesn’t soften what happened next. They plundered the Egyptians. That wealth did not vanish from the story. Chapters later, Israel brought gold, silver, bronze, yarn, fine linen, and skilled labor for the tabernacle. Exodus does not inventory which offerings came from Egypt, and some of the gold had already been turned into a calf. But Israel clearly left one kingdom carrying resources that could be placed in the service of another.

That’s the pattern for a tool built by one kingdom and used by another. Not refusal. Not naive adoption either. Take what’s useful, know exactly where it came from, and never forget what it’s for. A tool without a wielder who understands this defaults to whoever built it. AI literacy isn’t primarily a technical skill. It’s the discipline of carrying leverage out of Egypt without letting Egypt come with it.

3. Communication and Trust

A machine can draft a paragraph. It has read more sentences than any human who ever lived and can arrange them with real skill. What it cannot do is make a stranger trust the sentence enough to act on it.

Paul made the same point to Corinth about a trumpet. If the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who prepares for battle. He said it about tongues in worship, but the same rule holds wherever speech is meant to be understood. Unless it’s intelligible, it profits no one, and the speaker is just speaking into the air.

Clarity isn’t a style preference. It’s the difference between a sentence that moves someone and a sentence that evaporates the moment it’s read. AI can hand you clean grammar. It cannot hand you the years that taught you which sentence a particular reader will actually believe, and it cannot hand you the trust a reader has already extended to you before you wrote it.

4. Systems Thinking and Problem Framing

Isolated facts are cheap now too. A pattern connecting facts across history, economics, psychology, and theology is not, because a pattern like that requires someone who has actually walked all four rooms and remembers the floor plan of each one, and who can name the real problem before reaching for an answer to the wrong one.

Among the men who came to David at Hebron were two hundred from Issachar, described simply as men who understood the times and knew what Israel ought to do. Not the largest contingent in the chapter. Not the most decorated. The one whose contribution Scripture bothers to name is reading the moment correctly and knowing what to do about it.

That’s the skill. Not trivia. Not more input. The discipline of holding several fields in your head at once, long enough to see where they cross, and framing the real problem before anyone starts proposing solutions to the wrong one.

5. Character and Execution: Neither Idle Nor Unfruitful

None of the first four skills survive without this one holding them up. Discipline. Integrity. Patience. Courage.

A machine amplifies whoever is holding it. It doesn’t supply the character of the one holding it, and it was never going to.

Peter told his readers to add virtue to their faith, and knowledge to virtue, and self-control to knowledge, and perseverance to self-control, and godliness to perseverance, and brotherly affection to godliness, and love to brotherly affection.

Having these things, he said, and having them in abundance, is what keeps a person from being idle and unfruitful. Fruitfulness was never a talent. It was always a harvest, and a harvest requires someone who kept showing up to the field on the days nothing seemed to be growing.

AI can amplify output. Character decides whether the amplified output does good or harm, and no model weighs that for you.

The One That’s New

Four of these five would have mattered in any century a person cared to name. The fifth didn’t exist as a named skill a generation ago, and it only matters because of what it protects: the other four, kept intact, while a new tool moves through the room.

The right answer to a machine that generates convincing output at no cost isn’t to compete with it, and it isn’t to refuse it either. It’s to become the kind of person who can wield it without handing it your judgment, your trust, your discernment, or your character in exchange for speed.

You don’t get to skip this one by reading faster. The Human Edge is built to make these five deliberate instead of accidental — assessments, exercises, verification tools, the whole framework. Get it here.
